best_architecture: Orchestrator-worker fan-out/fan-in over a plan-time-validated dependency DAG, executed with asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) for structured concurrency. Layers: (1) PLANNING: LLM decomposes task -> dependency DAG -> Kahn's topological sort validates no cycles; (2) SCHEDULING: deterministic scheduler walks DAG, dispatches siblings in parallel immediately when dependencies complete; (3) CONCURRENCY CONTROL: dual gating -- asyncio.Semaphore bounds in-flight agents + dual RPM+TPM rate limiting with sliding-window/token-bucket + global token budget (~80% safety margin) shared via asyncio.Lock; (4) AGGREGATION: MoA-style -- parallel proposer agents generate candidates, aggregator synthesizes (optionally multi-layer); (5) INTER-AGENT COMMS: message-passing/state-handoff, not shared mutable state; each sub-agent returns condensed result to orchestrator. For Local-Claw specifically, the Gemma 4 MoE 4-bit orchestrator owns planning + scheduling + aggregation while Qwen2.5-Coder-32B specialist workers are the spawned sub-agents; because both models share a single RTX A6000 48GB, the Semaphore bound must be tuned to VRAM/KV-cache capacity (not arbitrarily high) and the orchestrator-worker handoff runs over the TS MCP server / Python MCP client (stdio JSON-RPC).

key_libraries: asyncio (Python stdlib, 3.11+) - TaskGroup for structured concurrency (auto-cancels siblings on failure, no orphaned tasks), Semaphore for bounding in-flight agents, Lock for guarding the shared token budget
aiolimiter (Python, >=1.1) - leaky-bucket AsyncLimiter for RPM/TPM rate limiting that integrates with the event loop
tenacity (Python, >=8.2) - async retry with exponential backoff + jitter for transient 429/5xx and worker timeouts

tiktoken (Python, >=0.7) - pre-flight token estimation so spawn decisions can respect the TPM/global budget before dispatch (note: use a Qwen/Gemma-appropriate tokenizer for exact counts; tiktoken is an approximation for non-OpenAI models)
graphlib (Python stdlib, 3.9+) - TopologicalSorter for cycle detection (raises CycleError) and ready-set scheduling (get_ready/done) of the dependency DAG
anyio (Python, >=4.0) - structured-concurrency task groups + capacity limiters; backend-agnostic alternative if not pinned to asyncio
networkx (Python, >=3.0) - DAG construction/validation, visualization, and ancestor/descendant queries during planning
langgraph (Python, >=0.2) - optional higher-level runtime providing Send() dynamic fan-out and reducer fan-in if not hand-rolling the scheduler
crewai (Python, >=0.40) - optional higher-level role-based orchestration if a batteries-included framework is preferred over the bespoke AsyncOrchestrator
pitfalls: Fire-and-forget tasks: using asyncio.gather (or bare create_task without a TaskGroup) means a failed sibling does NOT cancel the others -- orphaned coroutines survive their parent, leak VRAM/KV-cache, and silently keep burning the token budget. Production multi-agent data shows error rates climb from <0.5% (single agent) to >3% without structured cancellation. Use asyncio.TaskGroup so the `async with` block cannot exit until every spawned task has completed or been cancelled+cleaned-up.

Semaphore starvation / self-deadlock: blocking on `await sem.acquire()` for a child task that is itself spawned inside an already-saturated TaskGroup can deadlock (all permits held by parents waiting on children). Acquire the permit at the leaf worker, never around the fan-out site; size the Semaphore to real concurrency (for Local-Claw: VRAM/KV-cache capacity on the shared A6000, not an arbitrary large number).

Token-budget blind spot: spawning N agents without pre-estimating prompt+completion tokens busts the TPM/global budget mid-flight, causing cascading 429s and half-finished plans. Estimate tokens before dispatch (tiktoken/model tokenizer) and gate spawns against an ~80% safety-margin budget guarded by asyncio.Lock.

Shared mutable state corruption: parallel agents writing the same dict/list/result store without a lock (or without a reducer like LangGraph's operator.add) produces lost updates and races. Prefer message-passing handback to the orchestrator; if shared state is unavoidable, guard with asyncio.Lock or use append-only reducers.

DAG cycle deadlock: a dependency cycle not detected at plan time leaves agents waiting forever on each other. Validate with graphlib.TopologicalSorter.prepare() (raises CycleError) BEFORE any spawn -- fail fast at planning, never at runtime.

Context-window blowup: returning full raw outputs from N parallel workers into the orchestrator overflows its context (especially acute for a 4-bit Gemma orchestrator with a tight window). Each sub-agent must return a CONDENSED result (summary + artifacts/paths), not its entire transcript.

Silent agent failure: gather(return_exceptions=True) swallows a failed sub-agent and returns an Exception object in the results list, so an all-or-nothing task appears to succeed. Decide explicitly per-task whether failure is fatal (TaskGroup -> ExceptionGroup) or tolerated (and if tolerated, surface the failure in the aggregation, do not hide it).

Nested asyncio.run() deadlock: calling asyncio.run() (or loop.run_until_complete) from inside a coroutine already on a running loop raises 'RuntimeError: cannot be called from a running event loop' or hangs. Await coroutines directly; never re-enter the loop. Watch this at the Python MCP client boundary where sync and async code meet.

Over-spawning: launching 10+ workers for a task needing 2 causes GPU VRAM/KV-cache contention on the single A6000 and is SLOWER overall due to scheduling + context-switch overhead and rate-limit backpressure. Let the plan's DAG width (not a fixed max) drive parallelism, and cap it to the hardware's real concurrent-decode capacity.

Swallowing CancelledError: a worker that catches asyncio.CancelledError without re-raising breaks TaskGroup/timeout structured cancellation, so cancellation 'misbehaves' and tasks linger. Use try/finally for cleanup and always re-raise CancelledError after cleanup.
bdd_gherkin_scenarios:
Feature: Plan-time DAG validation
  Scenario: Dependency cycle is rejected before any agent is spawned
    Given a task decomposed into sub-tasks A, B, C
    And the dependency edges A->B, B->C, and C->A forming a cycle
    When the orchestrator validates the dependency DAG with a topological sort
    Then a CycleError is raised at planning time
    And no sub-agent worker is spawned
    And no tokens are consumed beyond the planning call

Feature: Parallel execution with dependency ordering
  Scenario: Independent siblings run concurrently while dependents wait
    Given a validated DAG where task C depends on both A and B but not on D
    And tasks A, B, and D have no unmet dependencies
    When the scheduler dispatches the ready set
    Then A, B, and D are spawned in parallel inside a single TaskGroup
    And C is not spawned until both A and B have completed successfully
    And if A raises an exception, B and D are cancelled and C is never spawned

Feature: Token-budget gating of spawns
  Scenario: A spawn that would exceed the global token budget is queued, not dispatched
    Given a global token budget with a remaining balance below the estimated cost of the next agent
    And a sliding-window TPM limiter that is currently saturated
    When the scheduler attempts to dispatch the next ready agent
    Then the spawn is rejected and the agent is held in a pending queue
    And the agent is dispatched only after enough budget/TPM headroom is released
    And no 429 / TPM-exceeded error is raised mid-flight

Feature: Mixture-of-Agents aggregation
  Scenario: N parallel proposals are synthesized into a single result
    Given a sub-task fanned out to N=3 proposer agents in parallel
    When all 3 proposers return their condensed candidate results
    Then an aggregator agent receives all 3 candidates
    And the aggregator produces exactly one synthesized result
    And only the synthesized result (not the raw 3 candidates) is handed back to the orchestrator context
optimal_implementation:
Build a single AsyncOrchestrator class. Core flow: plan -> validate DAG (fail fast) -> schedule ready set into a TaskGroup with Semaphore + token-budget gating -> each worker returns a CONDENSED result -> MoA-style aggregate. Use graphlib.TopologicalSorter for both cycle detection and ready-set scheduling.

```python
import asyncio, graphlib
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from aiolimiter import AsyncLimiter

@dataclass
class SubTask:
    id: str
    prompt: str
    deps: set[str] = field(default_factory=set)
    est_tokens: int = 0

@dataclass
class Result:           # condensed handback -- never the full transcript
    id: str
    summary: str
    artifacts: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    ok: bool = True

class TokenBudget:
    def __init__(self, total: int, margin: float = 0.8):
        self.remaining = int(total * margin)
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()
    async def reserve(self, n: int) -> bool:
        async with self._lock:
            if n > self.remaining:
                return False
            self.remaining -= n
            return True
    async def refund(self, n: int):
        async with self._lock:
            self.remaining += n

class AsyncOrchestrator:
    def __init__(self, max_inflight=4, rpm=60, tpm=90_000, budget=400_000):
        self.sem = asyncio.Semaphore(max_inflight)   # size to A6000 KV-cache capacity
        self.rpm = AsyncLimiter(rpm, 60)
        self.tpm = AsyncLimiter(tpm, 60)
        self.budget = TokenBudget(budget)
        self.results: dict[str, Result] = {}

    async def plan_and_dispatch(self, task: str) -> Result:
        subtasks = await self._plan(task)                 # LLM decomposition -> [SubTask]
        graph = {t.id: t.deps for t in subtasks}
        ts = graphlib.TopologicalSorter(graph)
        ts.prepare()                                       # raises CycleError -> fail fast, no spawn
        index = {t.id: t for t in subtasks}
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:              # structured concurrency: no orphans
            running: dict[str, asyncio.Task] = {}
            while ts.is_active():
                for tid in ts.get_ready():                 # all currently-unblocked siblings
                    running[tid] = tg.create_task(self._run_worker(index[tid]))
                done_id = await self._await_any(running)
                ts.done(done_id)
        return await self._aggregate(task, self.results)

    async def _run_worker(self, t: SubTask) -> str:
        # pre-flight budget + rate gating BEFORE spawning the model call
        while not await self.budget.reserve(t.est_tokens):
            await asyncio.sleep(0.5)                        # queued, not dispatched -> no TPM bust
        async with self.sem:                               # acquire at the leaf, never at fan-out
            async with self.rpm, self.tpm:
                try:
                    raw = await self._call_qwen_worker(t)  # specialist worker via MCP stdio JSON-RPC
                    self.results[t.id] = self._condense(t.id, raw)  # condensed handback
                except asyncio.CancelledError:
                    raise                                  # never swallow -> keeps TaskGroup correct
        return t.id

    async def _aggregate(self, task, results) -> Result:
        # MoA-style: feed condensed candidates to an aggregator agent (optionally multi-layer)
        return await self._call_aggregator(task, list(results.values()))
```

Key decisions to put in the spec: (1) TopologicalSorter.prepare() is the cycle gate -- runs before any spawn. (2) get_ready()/done() drive parallelism width from the DAG, not a hardcoded N. (3) Budget.reserve() under a Lock + AsyncLimiter for RPM/TPM is the dual gate; reserve BEFORE the model call, refund on failure. (4) Semaphore acquired inside the worker leaf, never around create_task. (5) _condense() enforces the condensed-result handback so the orchestrator context never overflows. (6) Use return_exceptions semantics consciously -- TaskGroup gives all-or-nothing via ExceptionGroup; if partial tolerance is wanted, catch inside _run_worker and mark Result(ok=False) so the aggregator sees the failure rather than it being hidden.
sota_improvements: Adopt LLMCompiler's plan-execute separation (compile the DAG once, dispatch many) instead of ReAct-style plan-per-step. This removes a planning LLM call per agent step -- a large latency/token win, and exactly what the static-DAG architecture already enables.

Tune MoA layer depth as an explicit quality/latency knob: more aggregation layers improve answer quality but add serial latency. For Local-Claw on a single A6000, start with 1 proposer layer + 1 aggregator and only deepen for hard tasks.

Speculative execution: start the most-likely DAG branches before their dependency outcomes are confirmed, then cancel-on-miss (TaskGroup makes cancellation clean). Trades extra tokens/VRAM for wall-clock latency on the critical path.

Use LangGraph's Send() API for dynamic runtime fan-out when the number of sub-tasks is unknown at plan time (e.g. 'one worker per file changed') -- it dispatches an arbitrary, runtime-determined number of parallel branches and fans in via an operator.add reducer, avoiding a brittle static DAG.

Exploit Python 3.13's improved ExceptionGroup introspection (and except* handling) so partial multi-agent failures can be triaged per-task in the aggregator rather than collapsing to a single exception.

Stream condensed results from sub-agents via async generators instead of batch-collecting all results, so the aggregator can begin synthesizing (and the user can see progress) as soon as the first proposers finish -- reduces perceived latency and orchestrator memory pressure.
